item.title: 6/30 Computational Vs. Physical Substrate Independence · Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness
item.dc:creator: Daniel Burger
item.description: Day 6 of 30: the first outcome of the Ontology, substrate independence, and why I mean physical rather than computational substrate independence: independent of biology, never of physics.
item.content:encoded:
Over the past three days, we discussed the goals of my Ontology. Today we start with the first of the three outcomes, which also sit right below the mission called hybrid mind uploading. It's called "substrate independence". What does this term mean in this context? In the Ontology, it's listed as a state, and the one line under it says: mind no longer tied to biological substrate. There's a widespread reading of these two words in which the substrate simply doesn't matter. That's no good frame of mind for somebody who wants to build one, and it's not what I mean. The trouble sits in "independence", as the word asks a question that it doesn't answer (the same way "transcending" did yesterday with its "beyond what?") => independent of what? And dependent on what instead?

On day four I said that a goal is something that we strive for and could fail at, and that an outcome is what follows either way, as long as we work on the mission ([Nov 2026]). We don't strive for substrate independence for its own sake. Each time a piece of brain gets swapped for an engineered one while the process keeps running, there's a bit less of the tissue that it started in. So it comes along with the work, and that's what the "either way" was about. It was never meant as a guarantee tho, as how far this can go is decided by physics and not by us. The three outcomes btw pair up with the three goals, one each. Solving death the way that this mission goes about it, so by (mechanistic) gradual replacement, brings a carrier that's no longer the biology that we were born with, which is substrate independence. Understanding consciousness brings augmented cognition, because what we can measure and model, we can at some point also steer and modify. And transcending humanity has the collective mind as its outcome, a term that I'm (as well) not happy with, and by far the weirdest of the three (but that's for its own day!).

So why substrate independence? I'll go through it in the order in which I went through it myself. The idea is older than the term. In 1950, Turing remarked that Babbage's Analytical Engine was meant to be purely mechanical, and that the fact that both our computers and our nerves work electrically therefore "cannot be of theoretical importance". Ten years later, Hilary Putnam figured out how to carry it over into the philosophy of mind (which is btw where functionalism starts). In "Minds and Machines" (1960) he compares mental states with the logical states of a Turing machine, and in "Psychological Predicates" (1967) he argues that pain can't be one particular state of the brain, as an octopus presumably feels pain with a brain that's built very differently, so pain has to be a functional state that many kinds of matter can realise. That's multiple realisability. And in 2003, Nick Bostrom wrote "substrate-independence" into his simulation argument. I'm not sure who used the term first, but he doesn't present it as his own, as he introduces it as "a common assumption in the philosophy of mind". Btw: What I find interesting is how much of what's relevant for my kind of work runs through Putnam => functionalism, multiple realisability, with them substrate independence, and even the brain in a vat (i.e. our functional brain isolation work at @eightsixscience). And I used the term in exactly this sense for years myself, e.g. in 2023, when I called one of my early aims "substrate-independent cognitive preservation" ([Nov 2023]).

That went on until this May, when I wrote down the founding commitments of classical mind uploading and "substrate independence as a working assumption" was one of them. That was the moment to finally put my name under it... and I couldn't go through with it. Whether because of Lerchner's paper on the Abstraction Fallacy ([deepmind.google]), the weeks of arguing about it afterwards ([Apr 2026]), or a sudden second-guessing of how calculating a process is supposed to be(!) that process, I filed it under the commitments that fix the answers in advance, and ended years' worth of using it ([May 2026]). Putnam, of all people, had been there looong before me. In 1988, he showed how to get any finite automaton out of pretty much any ordinary open system (it's in the appendix of "Representation and Reality"), which allows for a rock that runs whatever program you like. So if I take a lens from Putnam, then it's the one that he ended with.

Now, here I am again, with the same two words as the first outcome of my own Ontology. "They" always say that a mind goes wherever its computation goes, and the other "they" say that it only ever lives in living tissue (which is the only place where we've found one so far) => so I guess it's on me to say that nobody has shown either! Yeah, I know that this looks like I'm taking the assumption back in, but I'm only keeping its two words. And, tbh, as something that one arrives at (or doesn't), I like them a lot better than as something that one starts from. My take, however, is that I don't look at substrate independence through a functionalist lens, in the sense of having already subscribed to a theory of consciousness such as neurocomputational functionalism. What I start from is an observation => if we all have somewhat the same kind of experience across humans, then there must be some sort of multiple realisability, in the sense that we all do somewhat the same even tho our brains are all different. Sometimes there's a slow-growing tumour sitting right in somebody's speech area (i.e. a low-grade glioma), and it takes the brain a few years to "move" the speech area somewhere else, so that a surgeon can later cut where no textbook would let him (I'm simplifying the gradual reorganisation principle and serial lesion effect here btw, as this is also a topic for another day's meditation). Either way, I still find that rather wild. Of course, there's only so much that this can show, as it's living neural tissue taking over from living neural tissue. So the process doesn't seem to care which cells carry it. However, the substrate class is kind of the same in all of these cases, and that's the important question => does the process also not care what kind of thing carries it? I also have to correct myself. In June I wrote that because of the gliomas, bio-to-bio multiple realisability "must exist" in the biological brain, and I put a "hence substrate independence" in brackets behind it ([Jun 2026]). I'd still sign the part before the bracket. The bracket itself, not so...

Gualtiero Piccinini (a philosopher of computation) has this "mousetrap example" that I keep coming back to; he points out that while you can build a mousetrap in a variety of ways (in his terms this is what he calls multiple realisability), it still has to catch actual mice, while a computation doesn't "care" at all what its vehicles are made of – as long as they have the right degrees of freedom, which is what he calls "medium independence". Classical mind uploading turned out to need the second one for minds, and I found myself needing at most the first. The first one sits in every heart-lung machine btw, where the "lung" is a bundle of plastic fibres with blood on one side and gas on the other. There's no lung cell anywhere, and the blood comes out oxygenated anyway! Supposedly, nobody has managed that with a simulation of a lung yet (btw this work with artificial lungs vs what can be simulated as an input to a brain is again full-circle back to our work on functional brain isolation (= brains in vats)). What I'm wondering is if one can have the physics of the brain without the biology, or as I put it in September: a mechanistic piece of brain that does the same kind of physics as the real biological brain, and at the same time is computable in the sense that we can steer it ([Sep 2026]).

So in that modest sense, substrate independence already exists, as nature does it from tissue to tissue all the time. The question is if the thing can work without biology, and that's really two questions. Does physics allow it, so can any material other than living cells do the job? It's a question for experiments, and it has an awkward asymmetry => a single working case answers it with yes, whereas no number of failed attempts adds up to a no, as for that we'd have to understand why. And if physics allows it, what does it cost? The way that I think about this one, in terms of materials science: if the engineering effort is a scale with "running a SaaS company" on the left and "CERN and the LHC" on the right, where on that scale is showing that substrate independence is economically feasible, given the engineering complexity and efforts needed? I don't know. It can also come out as a yes from physics and a no from the economics, and then hybrid mind uploading becomes extreme biology instead (I've said so before: [Oct 2026]).

There's a kind of substrate independence in all of this that I think is the only one which can be an outcome, and I didn't have a word for it. So I'm putting a word in front that says what has to be kept. Computational substrate independence is what Bostrom and classical mind uploading mean => a mind depends only on the computation, so whatever runs it will do. Physical substrate independence is what I mean => a mind depends on what its carrier physically does, so whatever does the same will do, be it biological or not. And the other half has to be said out loud, as, in my view, a mind depends on its substrate a great deal => what it's supposed to become independent of is biology, and physics it never leaves. The physical version claims less than the computational one btw, as a material that does the same physics also runs the same computation along the way, but not the other way round.

There's a spectrum in this, and it's about how many materials can carry a mind. First, there's the tissue that you were born with, and nothing else will do. Then other living neural tissue will do as well, which is as far as the gliomas go. Then engineered living tissue, then at least one material that isn't alive (the candidate that I've been writing about is the alien neuron: [Sep 2026]), then many. And it could turn out that the class ends at living tissue. Then we'd have gone full circle => we set out to leave biology, and we arrive at building it (and then go towards maybe extreme biology by merging with genetically engineered fungi or something?).

That's basically the outcome => if we engineer this, then we'll have substrate independence, in the physical sense. A copy on another substrate shows nothing, as a copy would tell us that everything is fine in any case (day two). But if one takes a piece of a living brain and doesn't copy it, and instead lets an engineered piece take over its job while the rest keeps running, then this can show both that the piece does the job (because the experience is the same before, during and after the step, day four) and that it's still the same someone (again, because the process never stopped, if the hypothesis from day four holds). Careful tho: this is NOT Moravec's procedure, and it's not the setup of Chalmers's fading qualia either. Read "Mind Children" (1988) and pay close attention => the robot surgeon there, ostensibly doing the very same thing piece by piece, actually swaps each layer of the brain for a simulation of it, and Chalmers's silicon chips are defined as doing what a neuron does at its inputs and outputs. The actual difference, in both of these cases, is that what the brain does has already been coarse-grained (down to e.g. action potentials) before the first piece gets replaced, and for me that grain is the open part ([Jul 2026]).

Which leaves the question of what exactly has to be re-created. Earlier this year I started reading Romain Brette's "The Brain, in Theory" (on Lerchner's recommendation: [Sep 2026]), and its main point is one that an engineer doesn't like to hear: living organisms aren't engineered. So there's no plan of the brain that I could copy into another material, as nobody ever drew one. The brain is ultimately a physical thing, dynamical, organised and bounded, that goes forward in time (it's the carrier, and the process world-line is the activity that runs through it). So, however that activity is constrained by physics, originally via neuronal cells, the bet is that it's somehow engineerable with the same constraints. Neurons keep charges apart with membranes and let ions through them at some voltages and not at others, and all the while their chemistry rebuilds the very structure that the activity runs on. These are constraints, and I think that the brain is all about constraints. Not all of them sit inside the skull, btw, as a brain is always in a loop with something that it senses and acts on. Of course, it's hard to know where this list stops, and it's just as hard to know at which grain it starts (that's the lattice question that I've owed since day one: [Nov 2026]). So what has to be re-created in another material are these constraints, and the brain's parts only as far as they're needed for them. That's the quest, and THIS re-creation of the constraints is what I actually mean by substrate independence!

item.title: 5/30 Transcending Biology, but not Physics · Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness
item.dc:creator: Daniel Burger
item.description: Day 5 of 30: the third goal of the Ontology, renamed "transcend humanity": going beyond the limits that human biology sets for us, while the limits of physics stay where they are.
item.content:encoded:
The third and last goal of my Ontology is "transcend humanity". It comes after "solve death" (day three: [Nov 2026]) and "understand consciousness" (day four/yesterday: [Nov 2026]), and in the Ontology each of the three has a type => there's a "practical goal", a "theoretical one" and a "transformative one" => so today's goal is the one where the thing that changes is us (= the transformative one). It's also the one whose name I'm least happy with. I have three reasons for that, and two of them are why the goal has a new name as of today (until yesterday it was still called "human transcendence", which is also how it appears in yesterday's meditation).

The first reason is that the word is already taken. Taken literally it's harmless, as the Latin transcendere just means to climb beyond something. But theology, Kant and phenomenology have each claimed it (and prob. a bunch more I'm unaware of), and each of them gives a different answer to the only question that the word really asks, which is: beyond what? In theology, it's what lies beyond the world. With Kant, "transcendent" is what lies beyond any possible experience (please don't mix it up with his "transcendental", which is about the conditions of experience (until recently, I regularly mixed up those two terms!)). I came across the word mostly through Husserl tho. As far as I understand him, "transcendent" is said of whatever an experience is directed at without being a genuine ("reell" in German) part of that experience itself (Husserl's "Ideas I", §§41–44). His own example is a table => walking around it, I only ever see it from one side at a time (in adumbrations, Abschattung in German), so the table always is "more" than what's given to me right now, whereas the seeing itself is immanent and doesn't come in sides at all. Careful tho, as the table that I see is the very thing that appears, and no thing-in-itself that hides behind its appearances. Its transcendence lies in how it's given, which is never completely. So for Husserl, the answer to "beyond what?" is: beyond any experience that I have of the thing, and that's why there's always more of it to see.

Does my third goal want to get rid of that? No, and it couldn't. Husserl is quite clear that this has nothing to do with human eyes being weak, as any mind that perceives a thing gets it in adumbrations, and he says that this would hold even for God. So a mind with ten times my senses would still see the table from somewhere, and there would still be more of it to see. What can change is how much of that "more" a mind gets to, and with that I'm at my own answer. In the Ontology, it's us who go beyond something, namely the limits that human biology sets for us. And only those! The limits that physics sets stay where they are (it's the same line as on day three, where I stopped the definition of solving death at the universe itself => see the schematic that I created for today's post to visualise this). Death is one of the limits of biology, and it's the one that's important enough to have its own goal.

The second reason is the direction. "Human transcendence" can be read in two ways => either the human is the one who transcends, or the human is what gets transcended. The difference between "human transcendence" and "transcend humanity" lies exactly there, so in the direction of the change: the first one sounds like deepening and expanding what it means to be human from within, and the second one says that the human species gets left behind. I clearly mean the second one! I want to be exact about what gets left behind, as "humanity" is a word with several jobs too (the species, the people, and "being humane"). I mean the species, so the kind that we were born into, together with the limits of its biology (a species is a category of biology anyway, so the more of what carries you isn't biology anymore, the less that category says about you). I don't mean the person who goes beyond these limits, as that person is what I'm in this for (as I once put it in a reply: [Sep 2026]), I don't mean the people who'd rather stay (more on them below), and I certainly don't mean being humane. This is also where I go further than Julian Huxley, who made the word "transhumanism" known in the 1950s. His version is the from-within one: "man remaining man, but transcending himself" => and he meant it for the species as a whole. I start with the single someone (as on day one), and I drop the "remaining man" => it has to stay you, and it doesn't have to stay human.

So yes, this is basically about transhumanism, and the "trans" is the same one (beyond). Transhumanism is the position that it's possible and desirable to use technology in order to go beyond these limits, up to a point where the result may be called posthuman. I mean that in the transhumanist sense btw, so a being with capacities far beyond ours, and I don't mean the "posthumanism" of the humanities, which is a critique of humanism. Why don't I just call the goal "transhumanism" then? Because an -ism is something that you hold, and a goal is something that you reach, or don't. Which brings me to the third reason, and it's the simplest one => all goals in the Ontology are a "verb" + a "thing". Solving death and understanding consciousness are things that you do, whereas "human transcendence" was a noun, and it sounded like a state that one is in. That mismatch was more than cosmetics (don't forget, I do have diagnosed OCD!), as it's exactly what made me unsure for a while if this is a goal at all, or one of the outcomes of the Ontology. "Transcending humanity" is something that you do, and it even carries the answer to "beyond what?" in its name. I'm going to work through the limits themselves here, and then say more generally why this is a goal, and why it's the third one.

My first thought was that when death is solved, what it means to be human will have changed so drastically that this alone is the transcendence (which is true btw!). I then had to point out to myself that while this takes death out of the category of things that one simply has to accept, it still leaves the third goal in the category of the first one, just in other words. And then I realised that I didn't actually know what else there was. I had a goal sitting in my own Ontology that I couldn't spell out. I found that rather bizarre. So let me start with where the limits come from ... the ones that I mean all come from the thing that carries us, and ours came with the biology that we were born into, and when you then want to know who picked exactly these, you have to go and ask evolution, or you just stand there with a big "why these?!". The usual answer is that a limit was simply the cheaper way to stay alive, and it never occurred to anybody to change it afterwards. Evolution has been at this for a few billion years. I'm not sure when it last asked the one who's alive right now what they'd like to experience, but I'd guess never (that's the generational route from day one again). So I'm wondering how many of these limits we even notice. Death is the one that everybody knows. With the others it took us ages to even notice them, if we did at all. And along the same lines, I suspect that there are limits which are really hard to notice from the inside, as we never had it any other way! Humans see through a sort of slit. If you've seen a chart of the electromagnetic spectrum, you may have noticed the thin coloured stripe in it, which looks sort of like somebody forgot to colour in the rest. Vision is basically that stripe, so roughly one octave out of everything that's there. Of course, there's only so much that a body can do about its own limits. Often even the senses that we do have need help before they're of any use at night or over a distance. Some species evolved to specialise in exactly that; for instance, bats and dolphins find their way around by listening to their own echoes. Humans, with rather unspecialised senses and a skull that only fits so much, learned other ways to get around their limits. One such way is the telescope. If you point the right one at the sky, it'll show you infrared, translated into the colours that you can see anyway. But what you get is still a picture in the old colours, as everybody who has looked at a false-colour image knows. A notebook also helps, as it keeps what memory doesn't (remembering something is never like being there again, and I'll come back to this one in a second (trust me on that one, this one will be special!)). And a third way around a limit is the spacesuit, which takes along the narrow range of temperature and pressure that a body survives. All three go around a limit and leave it where it was, namely in the thing that carries the experience (the limit of being one mind, closed off from every other one, I'm leaving out today, as it needs its own day).

Now, a carrier that gets built (and is no longer born) can be built differently. That's the whole point => a built substrate is a steerable one, which is why I wrote in September that the ambition extends well beyond life extension ([Sep 2026]), and why I once called "steerable phenomenology" the thing that the transhumanist has long dreamt of without once having thought it ([Sep 2026]). Where there's a gradual replacement, there's that choice again for every single part. Each time a piece of tissue gets swapped for something engineered (that's the mechanistic gradual replacement from day three, so the core of hybrid mind uploading (which will also receive it's on meditation day in the coming weeks)), there's a bit of the carrier that doesn't have to repeat every limit of the tissue that it replaced. Where there's freedom like this, the substrate becomes steerable, and with it, bit by bit, the phenomenology (and I mean phenomenology, not just phenomenal space or qualia, but actually phenomenology). Some of what the tissue does – especially the storing – comes with losses that we're so used to that we hardly count them as limits. Memory compresses what it stores, as metabolism and physical space in the brain are limited, and it rebuilds what it recalls, with the gaps filled in from priors and context. Presumably everybody has noticed at some point that if they go back to a day that mattered to them, what comes back is both fainter and less reliable than the day itself was. (That's why remembering never feels like actually and truly being there)

It's only this January that I properly worked through what a built substrate could do about this, in a working document called "Synthetic Substrates and the Destruction of the Forward Arrow of Personal Time", which leans on Lyre's neurophenomenal structuralism (I never published this document because I was always afraid it would sound too crackpot-like before I had at least some directionally empirical insights into it). The thesis in there is that this limit is a contingent one of biological storage and no principled one => if a substrate took an experience and didn't compress it, but instead stored it whole, this would yield a memory that's both as rich as the experience was (because nothing got lost at the storing) and the same every time (again, because nothing has to be rebuilt at the recall). This is what I called "lossless Q-storage" there in the doc, with the "Q" standing for what an experience is like. Of course, while such a substrate would make remembering as rich as experiencing, allowing for a personal time that one can traverse instead of getting pushed through it, there is no guarantee that it can be built at all (that's an open engineering question, the typical case of: it works in principle, but not in practice). Since it only changes what gets played back, there's also just no time travel in it, compared to what the title may suggest: the substrate itself still runs forward, like a video player that "ages" normally while whatever it plays can be rewound. It takes physics as it is, limits included. (How one would still tell reliving from living with a memory like that is another open question in there. In the Ontology, all of this sits under augmented cognition btw => another day!)

So I think of the third goal as a related but distinct idea, that solving death lifts one limit of biology (the one that everybody knows), and that it will take a much longer process, which may or may not work out in the end, to get beyond the other ones. Often when I say "the other ones", I simply mean where a mind can exist, or what it can do and keep, or how it's connected to other minds (i.e. hivemind-ism). The Ontology has names for where these lead, which are its three outcomes: substrate independence, augmented cognition and collective mind (each of them gets its own day). There is a kind of change that I think will come first, and the Ontology already has a word for it. My first impulse is to call all of it augmentation, after the plain sense of the word, so more of what a mind already does (seeing more, keeping more, holding more, etc.), which can be checked against what that mind did before. But in the interest of not underselling it, I'm inclined to add that the memory example already goes further than that, as keeping a bit more is augmentation, and a personal time that one can traverse would be an experience that no human has ever had, so a change of kind. (If that far end can be reached, I don't know)

My main way of keeping the three goals apart rests on the process world-line, so if solving death keeps it going, and understanding consciousness lets us measure (and later steer) what runs along it, then transcending humanity is what lets that same world-line outgrow the limits that it was born with. And "that same" is the part where hybrid mind uploading goes a different way than the transhumanism that I came from, so classical mind uploading. There, people figured that one could isolate the pattern from the rest of the brain, which would allow for minds that get scanned, copied and upgraded like software. If the pattern is all that you are, you can run it wherever you like, allowing for transcendence in a single step, skipping the "slow" hybrid state in between. The price of this shortcut comes in two parts. First, when using a copy in order to transcend, we lose the one who was supposed to do the transcending, as death is the irreversible end of a conscious process world-line (day three), and that's what happens to the original's process, however good the copy is. Second, we become blind to that very loss, to the point where everybody, the copy included, would describe what happened as a transcendence, rather than as a death with a very capable newcomer right after it (a new someone with a head start, the same way a baby is a new world-line). So between similarity and continuity, I pick continuity! My Ontology says the same about world-line fidelity btw: it never breaks, and nothing gets traded against it (enhancement included). You may change a great deal on the way, but there can't be a moment at which one stops and another one takes over. And to be careful about what I'm claiming here: at every single step it has to be still you (the "continuer"), which is a different claim from "you'll stay the way you are" (you won't, and you didn't so far either, as the five-year-old you wouldn't recognise much), and it's also no promise about where you end up. That the world-line really goes on through such changes is a hypothesis, as I said yesterday, and it still gets its own day.

I'm having some trouble saying what exactly makes this a goal and no outcome, but here's a first attempt. Transcending humanity will tend to look like an outcome, as an engineered carrier comes with other limits than a biological one, whether anybody plans for that or not. This naturally makes it harder to say what's left to strive for, and it takes some honesty on my side, as I may have filed an outcome under the goals (yesterday's definitions were: a goal is something that we strive for and could fail at, and an outcome is what follows either way, as long as we work on the mission). But it's not merely an outcome. You could have the state, the capability and the topology that the three outcomes of the Ontology describe, and still be nowhere close to anybody having transcended anything, as the minds that have them could all be replacements, or nobody might have gone at all (which would be a decision too btw, as with a built carrier, keeping a limit is as much a choice as moving it). So what follows either way is only that it becomes possible, and the goal is that we get there, as the ones that we are.

Transcending humanity is also the last of the three for a reason (it's no ranking by importance, btw). First, it needs the engineered carrier that solving death brings – that's where the limits become steerable, and it's what the reply from above means with "solve death, augmentation comes next". Second, it needs the understanding of consciousness, and more of it than solving death does. By changing the experience on purpose instead of keeping it the same, an augmentation step takes away the marker that such a replacement step still has (the same experience before and during as well as after) and what has to be shown is that it's the same process, now having a different experience. Without that, nobody could tell transcendence from replacement, not even the one who comes out of it. That's a harder check than yesterday's, and I don't have it yet.

And what does all of this mean for humanity, and now I mean the people? Of course, I don't really know where to stop with that question, and I know even less where to start. Today's meditation could easily be double the length (respect to everyone who is still reading this, I've sometimes got the feeling that I'm the first and last person to read this sentence). Ideally, whoever builds this would attend to the people who want none of it, and then try to leave their lives exactly as good (or bad?) as they are. The first goal says "no one has to end" and it never said that nobody is allowed to(!). In the same way, this one says that no one has to stay within the limits of biology, and it doesn't say that anybody has to leave them. Nothing matters except to someone conscious, and ordinary biological consciousness already meets that condition (day one: [Nov 2026]), so a life inside these limits is no lesser one, and transcending them is no condition for anything. (And if some get access first, that's potentially a problem. And if some get pushed into it, that's an even bigger one. But I have to park both of them for today. I only wanted to say what the goal says. That's all. How we live next to people who chose differently (which takes patience on both sides, and we're currently quite bad at it) has to come later)

Another difficulty that this goal raises is that a humanity which "transcends" via copies has simply ended, with something very convincing left behind, although this one can be avoided by not taking the shortcut from above. That's the risk that I take most seriously btw, and it's why I keep saying that classical mind uploading could be a Great Filter ([Jan 2026]). Why shouldn't there be people who'd rather stay inside the limits of biology, or who only take a part of what's possible? It's very possible that the from-within version, the one that Huxley wanted for all of us, is what many will pick, e.g. because they simply like being human, but then do we tell the ones who want to leave that they have to stay as well? I don't see why both couldn't be around at the same time. In particular, "enabling a new state of humanity", which I listed among the original goals of mind uploading on day two, still seems right to me, with the stress on the "of" => a new state OF humanity is only one if it's still the same people who are in that state, whatever happens to the species.

Will it stay the third goal? The goal, yes. The name I've just changed, and I'm not sure that it was for the last time, as it's still the weakest of the three, and "transcending" keeps borrowing the glow of its religious sense. The oldest word for all of this that I know of is Dante's "trasumanar" (first canto of the Paradiso), and there it's what happens to him as he rises into heaven. No matter how carefully I define "transcending"; there's always a chance that somebody somewhere hears the old use in it (that's the "borrowed-word problem" from day two of this meditation series; where a word's old use quietly decides what has to be true in the new place!). If I borrow a word that's at home in heaven, then I imply that I mean what it meant there: that perfection is waiting on the other side, that leaving the world behind is what this is about, and that the limits of physics go together with the ones of biology. Or that if only a better mind looked at the table, it would finally get seen from all sides. I mean none of that, and if the name changes again, what's behind the three names should stay as it is. item.title: 4/30 Measurements, Models and Theories · Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness
item.dc:creator: Daniel Burger
item.description: Day 4 of 30: the second goal of the Ontology, understand consciousness, and why measurement comes before models and models before any theory of what consciousness is.
item.content:encoded:
The second goal of the Ontology is simply called "understand consciousness". To be clear about which goals I mean: the Ontology ([Sep 2026]) has three of them, which are "solve death" (that was yesterday: [Nov 2026]), understand consciousness and human transcendence, and they're no longer identical with the original goals of mind uploading that I listed on day two. What I mean by this second one is that in order to make hybrid mind uploading work as a mission towards the vision of synthetic consciousness, one will definitely have to solve death, as the first goal, but probably, and that's a big probably, also understand consciousness. I do believe that in the coming years, especially due to the progress in artificial intelligence, we will see a great "rigorisation of science", and especially of the consciousness sciences as well. The reason being that we can now reason across hundreds of papers, or across whole piles of data, at the same time, and with that we uncover many of the inconsistencies in thinking and in terminology, and also the data flaws and mistakes that we've made in science up to this point (computational philosophy is basically the same move btw). In the consciousness sciences, this matters even more, as that field can't hide its measurement problem and is being forced to work out what even counts as a test of a theory ([Oct 2026]). You can already see the first signs of it btw, e.g. in the adversarial collaborations, where theories with conflicting predictions get tested against each other. I also assume that the overfocus on neurocomputational functionalism will fade away, as right now it's mostly held as a faith rather than tested as a hypothesis ([Jul 2026]), and that we'll look back at those days and wonder how quickly we anthropomorphised anything that outputs "I'm angry" (the angry chair from an earlier tweet: [Feb 2026]).

And due to this rigorisation, I do expect that we'll get somewhere with consciousness. Probably not to a theory, but probably to a model, or at least to a measurement theory, and as these three get mixed up all the time, let me say how I use them (for the first one, see Johannes Kleiner and his workshop "Towards a Measurement Theory for Consciousness Science": [Feb 2026]). A measurement theory is the most "modest" of the three, as it only tells you what kind of data count at all (e.g. reports, behaviour, neural markers, etc.), and how to read that data as experience => it doesn't say why. With a model, you can already predict which experience goes with which physical state. And a theory, well, that would say what consciousness is and why there is any of it in the first place. Why would one precede the other? Because you can calibrate well before you can explain. So what I expect is measurement first, within years, then predictive models, and a theory of what consciousness is may never be reachable by science at all. And no, measurement doesn't come for free either, as what you think consciousness is already shapes what you accept as a measurement of it (that's Birch's point: [Apr 2026]), so it's measurement before a full theory, with the two correcting each other in turns.

The nuanced difference here, and why this is in the Ontology at all, is that while working on what I nowadays call biomimetic neuromorphics (it takes the slot that whole brain emulation has in classical mind uploading, but in hybrid mind uploading), we do what I call "consciousness engineering" (which is also the name of the Frontiers Research Topic that I co-organised: [May 2026]). Meaning: we engineer with matter that we try to couple and integrate with the biological brain, so that experience extends across both parts (that's what I mean by "bridging" phenomenal consciousness), with the aim of ultimately letting it "host" synthetic consciousness. And my bet is that measurement theories, and maybe even models of consciousness, will emerge from exactly this kind of work. And yes, understanding consciousness is such a huge goal, so why is it "only" the second one? I order the three goals by what depends on what (and no longer by importance): solving death is what all of this is for, understanding consciousness is what's needed to check that death really got solved (more on that in a second), and human transcendence, the third goal (and the meditation for tomorrow!), presupposes both, as it's even more far-reaching than solving death, comes at, or shortly after, the inflexion point of solving death, and is actually coupled with some of the outcomes of the Ontology. I do make a difference between goals and outcomes btw: a goal is something that we strive for and could fail at, and an outcome is what follows either way, as long as we work on the mission. So why isn't understanding consciousness just an outcome then? My first answer was "because we should strive to do that", which is no reason yet. The reason is that hybrid mind uploading can sidestep a theory of consciousness when it comes to building the thing that carries the process, but it can't sidestep measuring, as without a way to tell that experience is still there, and that it's still this experience, we could never know if the mission succeeded (that's the point that I left open yesterday btw, that it has to be shown physically if a world-line really went on). Hence a goal, at least up to the level of measurement, and no mere outcome.

I always say that the whole point of hybrid mind uploading is to not need a theory of consciousness in order to make it work, or to have confidence in it (as in classical mind uploading via simulations, where one has to believe that it's going to work due to a theory of consciousness, an unproven one, which might be wrong), but to actually sidestep it. So not ignoring the problem, but sidestepping it! Ignoring the theories completely would be insanity, as you'd end up assuming one anyway, just without noticing ([Oct 2026]). What sidestepping means is that hybrid mind uploading doesn't let its success depend on any single theory of consciousness being the only true one. It assumes a few things openly (the process world-line is one of them => I hold it as a hypothesis, and yes, yet again, this is for another meditations challenge day!), and the idea is that rival theories become predictions that a measurement can test. So instead of betting on just a single one of them, the route should be built in a way so the question can be checked gradually/step by step. It's, e.g. similar to how steam engines came before thermodynamics (Newcomen had his engine running in 1712, and Carnot explained what such an engine does in 1824), or to how Faraday had a wire rotating around a magnet in 1821, the first electric motor basically, long before anybody knew what an electron is (Thomson, 1897). You don't need to understand electrons in order to build an electric motor. The analogy breaks at one place tho, and well, yes, of course it's the place that matters a lot: you can see from the outside that a motor works; it turns. You can't see from the outside that a world-line went on. And that's exactly why the measuring part can't be sidestepped => what has to be shown is the same experience before, during and after a replacement step, from the reports as well as from physical markers.

It's all about doing something useful, and for doing something useful we're using an engineering mindset and not a science mindset (hence clearly consciousness engineering, and not consciousness science). However, I do think that this goal in the Ontology is where the science can slip back in a bit, as, like I said earlier, one can probably solve the measurement problem of consciousness with this work, or at least contribute heavily towards it, and then, with that, maybe even go towards very pragmatic modelling of consciousness. The example from another discipline that fits best here is temperature, I think. Thermometers as well as fixed scales (Fahrenheit, 1724) were around long before a kinetic theory explained what temperature even is (1850s–1870s). Hasok Chang showed in "Inventing Temperature" how people got out of this circle there as you can't calibrate a thermometer without knowing what temperature really is (and you can't know what temperature is without a thermometer in the first place, so every round of measuring corrected the concept, and also the other way around). So, did we achieve the goal of "understand consciousness" when we "only" have a model of consciousness instead of a theory? Well, not really, I guess? Or let me be more exact, as "understand" comes in three levels for me => measuring it, modelling it and explaining it. The goal counts as reached at the second level, and the third one is the horizon, where I don't know if science can ever get to. Why the second and not already the first? Because measuring only tells you afterwards, and for a step that you can't undo you want to know before, so the model that I'm asking for has to be able to tell me before a replacement step if the experience will change.

Trying to answer this question properly is a Pandora's box tho, or rather a deep tunnel of issues that we're opening here (which is btw kind of on purpose why I added this goal to the Ontology). The reason being: what is a theory of consciousness even? It might be that the scientific method as we have it isn't equipped to answer such questions, as it might sit on the same level of investigation as "what is an electron?", "why is there an electron?" and "why is there stuff rather than no stuff?". Careful though, as these are three different questions and I shouldn't ask them in one breath: the first one is a question for physics, the second one asks why the laws are as they are, and the third one is Leibniz's question. Science is great at the first kind, and my worry is that a theory of what consciousness is belongs to the other two, so basically just one level above absolute explanatory nihilism (the point where the only answer left is "it just is"), and that you slowly converge towards metaphysics instead of physics there, and that it might never be testable. Maybe a theory of consciousness will always be poetry, in the sense in which Bohr said that when it comes to atoms, language can be used only as in poetry ([Oct 2026]), and never actually within the realm of the scientific method (which is no insult to the people who describe experience carefully btw, that's rigorous work). So maybe we're just left with models of consciousness, in order to make useful predictions, which is basically what all of science does, and what the big break in physics was about back then when Bohr and Einstein had their discussion about quantum physics: is the theory complete and does it describe what's really there, or is a wave function "just" a model for us to predict with? So, if we have a really good model of consciousness, we might just say that this is useful enough (esp. in engineering, e.g. for hybrid mind uploading within biomimetic neuromorphics) to say that "we indeed understand consciousness now". And I think that this is legit and not a cheap way out. For a very "Wittgensteinian reason": the meaning of a word like "understand" isn't fixed in advance. What "fixes" it is how we're using it. We say that a pupil understands a rule when he knows how to go on (that's from his Philosophical Investigations, §§143–155). Understanding in the engineer's use of the word in that sense is a model that allows us to measure, predict, but also steer experience across a replacement step. There is another use that may well remain open => the one that asks why there is experience at all! I put this goal into the Ontology to keep both uses in view (in my first draft I ended with "we're just humans, writing down our higher-dimensional thoughts as lower-dimensional language", but that's the picture of the early Wittgenstein, which he later gave up himself).

item.title: 3/30 Solving Death · Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness
item.dc:creator: Daniel Burger
item.description: Day 3 of 30: why I want to solve death, cause versus reason, the lightbulb analogy and where it breaks, and the deprivation view of why death is bad for the one who dies.
item.content:encoded:
I run a company called @eightsixscience, where we try to functionally isolate the brain ([Sep 2026]); in other words, we take living brains out of their bodies and keep them alive outside their original bodies for as long as possible. We have early success in doing so in rodents; we're working toward the same for a large-animal brain, and ultimately we want to do this for humans as well. When I tell people about this – friends, family, people I meet at scientific conferences, investors or also just random people I meet throughout life (e.g. my hairdresser, who I recently told what exactly I'm doing) – I usually get the one question that gets asked most: "Why are you doing this?" I simply answer: "Because I want to solve death, and functionally isolating brains is, according to my own reasoning, the most pragmatic route towards that goal". And then usually the question comes right after: "But, why? Why do you want to solve death?"

The short answer, before I ramble on for way too long: it's complicated, and no, I still don't have a clean one after ≈10 years of getting asked. I can tell you why death is bad for the one who dies; that part I'm fairly sure about. But why exactly me, why I can't put this thing down again? No idea, and it gets worse the longer I think about it – same as with "what has to be true along the way" as well as "when would we even call it solved"; because every time I answer one of those, I do actually end up with a new question instead: what even is a world-line, what makes a continuation worth having, and so on (which is btw exactly why solving death is one of the three hard goals that the mission has to achieve in the Ontology).

Depending on who asks, I've come to several answers over the years, depending on the person, the context, and the time available. It ranges from personal upbringing reasons, e.g. my mom going through the Yugoslav wars and telling me stories as a child about all the terrible things that she had seen (hence developing a morbid and catastrophic view on death early on), or that I was depressed as a teenager and prob read the wrong kinds of books in a row that led me, back then, towards thinking that death is actually the only answer (that phase is long over btw). Now, the thing is, and I have to be strict with myself here, that both of these stories answer a question that nobody asked. When somebody asks me "why do you want this?", they could mean "what made you want it?" or they could mean "what makes it worth wanting?". Those are actually two very different things => the first one is a cause and the second one a reason (and my mom's stories and my teenage bookshelf are e.g. obv causes). They tell you how I ended up with death as my main topic. But if the goal itself is any good: they don't tell you at all (and tbh, they also can't tell you that it's bad. People do try that one, and it's the genetic fallacy, just used in the other direction!). The usual comeback here is "so it's just your fear of death talking", and I think that one deserves an honest answer: yes, maybe, I even posted a quote once saying that one of the principal things that moves people is the terror of death ([Oct 2024]). But you can play the exact same game with the other side! For basically all of human history there was nothing, like really nothing, that anybody could do about it, so what else would you do other than making your peace with it (Elster calls this adaptive preferences, or just "sour grapes"). So fine, my wish can be explained away, but so can everybody else's acceptance, and then explaining away doesn't decide anything here.

Other avenues of explanation are usually more mythological, as in: death always seemed to be humanity's forbidden fruit and life in general; it's the one great barrier one shall not pass, and if you're curious, you obviously love to explore that boundary. Again, curiosity is a cause and no reason, but the "shall not pass" part deserves a closer look, as nearly every culture has a story that warns you about going there (e.g. Gilgamesh loses his plant of youth to a snake, and Tithonus gets his eternal life without the eternal youth). Even my own "forbidden fruit" picture fits btw, as in Genesis the forbidden fruit is strictly speaking knowledge, and it's the tree of life that gets guarded afterwards, so that nobody eats from it and lives forever. People sometimes hand me these stories as an argument, as in "humanity has always known that this is a bad idea". I read them as the wisdom of a time in which nothing could be done, so they belong to the same making-peace as above, and if you look closely, what most of them warn against is a bad version of not having to die (ageing forever, being alone forever), which nobody is asking for. The one reading that's left is the hubris one, that it's against the order of things, and "the order of things" is no argument by itself, as the night is part of that order as well, which brings me to the lightbulbs.

So, more societally as an explanation, one of the analogies I've recently been bringing up during conversations is the example of pitching the lightbulb in front of people working on candles in the early 1800s. Instead of accepting the limitations of candles for brightening up the night, which is what we've done for thousands of years as Homo sapiens, why not go beyond those limits by inventing magically glowing things called lightbulbs, whose light doesn't have to burn down the way a candle does? It's coming from a totally different angle to solve the same problem, which is: keep it bright for as long as you want (you see the analogies I'm drawing slowly creeping in!). When working on lightbulbs, you don't iterate on candles; you approach it with different things. And that's the beauty, because the upshot of solving "it being bright at night, against nature's reason to make it dark at night due to the earth blocking the sunlight" is that we ultimately needed to work on electricity, have constant access to electricity, DC then AC, and this led towards the electrification of a bunch of things, and ultimately also to the digital computer, and then AI, AGI and superintelligence (quite literally btw: the "Edison effect" was found inside a lightbulb in the early 1880s, Fleming turned it into the first vacuum tube in 1904, and the first electronic computers were rooms full of the descendants of that tube). Who would have thought that the people working on lightbulbs back in the day were working on this uphill technology with a tail that leads us towards superintelligence? I usually say that solving death kind of feels like this nowadays. It seems like, for the first time, we have enough of the technology and knowledge to start seriously, so let's try. The upshot of this is unknown, and nobody can predict it; we can only guess. A few people like Nikola Tesla predicted, quite accurately, some future scenarios back then, but I don't think this is possible anymore, and I don't know anything about what the future has in store for us when we solve death, other than that solving death is just step one and that life in a post-death society will be stranger than we can imagine ([Oct 2025]).

I used to end this pitch with "but whatever it is, it must be net positive, otherwise it will be filtered out either way" (basically "dialectic" in society), and I have to take that part back, as it doesn't survive my own scrutiny. Bad things can stick around for a very long time before a society filters them out, and some things do the filtering on us instead. So let me say what I think the analogy really gives me. It shows the kind of move, as the improvement path of the candle (better wax, better wicks) never arrives at the lightbulb, and the candle here is biology. You can make it burn longer, and I'm all for that, but, e.g. reversing ageing halts the dying and doesn't solve death, as you can still get hit by a bus ([Sep 2026]). It also shows that the upshots came through the infrastructure that the solution needed (electricity), which nobody working on it could foresee, and I expect the same here, as you can't work on this without understanding and engineering the thing that carries consciousness. And it takes care of the "order of things" from above, as nobody thinks today that the lightbulb was an offence against the night. Now, does any of this tell me that the result will be good? No, and no analogy ever could; I mean, it's lightbulbs. And there's one place where my nice analogy just falls apart, and it's kind of the most important place => continuity. If a lightbulb is off and you swap it for a new one, nobody cares; the light is simply "on again". With a consciousness, that's the whole difference between going on and being replaced (the 4D process world-line gets its own day). And what's left of my "it must be net positive" is weaker; I'm afraid => the direct effect is good if death is bad for the one who dies (next paragraph), and for everything that comes after that, I really don't know.

Now, to come back, I technically have even more examples, and they range from the personal "life is great, death is bad, so I want more of life" to the very logical reasons as described in one of the earlier meditations ([Nov 2026]), to the very visionary views such as the lightbulb scenario above. Out of these, the logical one is the one that carries the most weight for me (it's the central reason, if you want), so I'll go through it once more, slowly. It starts with the thing from day one => nothing matters except to someone conscious. Death is the irreversible end of a conscious process world-line, so when such a world-line ends, everything that would have come after just doesn't happen for the someone that this world-line is, and if that would have been worth having, then missing out on it is bad for that someone (that's Nagel's deprivation view; I didn't invent this). The "worth having" matters a lot btw, as it's the reason why the goal in the Ontology says "no one has to end" and why it never said, "no one is allowed to end". Also, yes, there are some well-known objections (e.g. Epicurus, Lucretius, "death gives life its meaning", "we have to make room", and so on, etc.), but I'll potentially talk about those things on another day, especially as today's meditation is getting way too long already...

OK, so that's the "why-is-death-bad"-part, and I think it holds up. But did you notice? I still haven't answered the question, as "why is death bad" and "why do YOU want to solve it" are just two different questions, and the second one is so much harder, which is kind of the main thing that I want to deliver today. A person can have every reason in their hands and yet still not know exactly why they actually want it. Arguments don't make people magically want things (on that part, Hume was right!). Plenty of people nod at every single step above and then go on with their lives as if nothing happened. So why do I want to solve death? Well, I don't know. Personal urge? I guess this is where the causes from the beginning come back in, as the reason is there for everybody, and my mom's stories and the wrong books are why I'm one of the people who can't put it down again. To put it simply: I will try doing so, otherwise I'll die either way, so who cares? That last part might sound like a joke, but I think there's actually a real argument hiding in it. Say nothing changes => I die, like everybody before me, that's the baseline. Say I try, and it doesn't work out => I die as well, so the same thing, except that there's whatever the attempt produced along the way. And if I try and it does work (for me, I mean), then that's obviously better, and if it only works for the people after me, then it's a gain for them and none for me, I'm aware of that. So for me, as far as I can see, trying is at least as good as not trying. There are two "buts" though. The attempt shouldn't cost me a life that I'd rather have lived (it doesn't – I love this work), and nothing worse than simply dying should be reachable along the way, and that second one doesn't come for free, nothing guarantees it, somebody has to design for it blabla. I know of two such outcomes on my own route btw. A conscious brain that's kept going without any input, without any way to act and without anything that protects it from suffering would be one of them, and I'd call that worse than death (more on that below). The other one is a "solution" that only produces a copy, or something that merely behaves like me, which people would walk into believing that they'd go on, and which is the reason why I only want engineering means that need no metaphysical gambling ([Nov 2025]), as that would be worse than no solution at all.

"Solving death" is one of the three goals of the Ontology ([Sep 2026]), and with the above in place I can say more exactly what it implies. The Ontology has a vision (synthetic consciousness, so consciousness that no longer has to end, which is a state), a mission (hybrid mind uploading, which is the undertaking) and the goals, which are what the mission has to achieve. Now, somebody who read day one carefully could say: wait, isn't "solving death" just the vision again, in other words? I asked myself the same, and I think it isn't, and the easiest way to see it is this => imagine that there's exactly one synthetic consciousness around, and everybody else still dies like today. Then you'd have a first instance of the vision, and you'd be nowhere near the goal. So with the vision, I'm talking about a state that should exist at all, and with the goal, I mean every single someone: your world-line doesn't have to end, and neither does anybody else's. It's also the one part that you can share with me without sharing my route, btw, as somebody who works on purely biological ways has the same goal (even if I think that biology alone can't get them there) and nothing else of the Ontology in common with me.

What is death? => the irreversible end of a conscious process world-line. In last year's article ([May 2025]) I called it the irreversible destruction of the physical and dynamic processes of consciousness, which is the same thing seen from the engineering side. And the one word in there that I had to think about the longest is "irreversible", because, well, irreversible according to whom, and when? A stopped heart was the end until CPR showed up. Then the end got moved into the brain, and nowadays surgeons cool brains down until the EEG is flat (nuanced detail: until EEG electrodes can't measure anything meaningful anymore!) and people still wake up as themselves, so medicine keeps pushing the point where a stop turns into an end further out (where exactly that point is, is for the meditation day on the 4D process world-line). I mean the strict version => death is the end that can't be undone by anything that physics allows. This also implies that "solving death" can never be about bringing somebody back from an end, only about never letting a stop turn into one (yes, this has implications for biostasis, where the open question is exactly if it's a stop or an end!). Preventing that point from ever being reached is the problem that I mean, and that one is an engineering problem ([Jan 2025]).

What is solving death? Solving meaning that death does not occur in the universe anymore? Well, not really. You can solve a thing practically, and it can still happen. We "solved flying" by making things fly (Icarus didn't stop anybody in the end), but you can still have things meant to fly that cannot fly, and planes that come down. Meaning, you can solve death, and death can still occur in the universe. The analogy only goes so far btw, as a steady crash rate is fine for flying and exactly not enough for death. I quickly discussed this on day one, and there's a big difference here that I want to be exact about, as three things get mixed up all the time. Step zero is to stop dying. If you halt the dying (the ageing and e.g. the failing organs), you get what one might call amortality => no clock in you runs out by itself anymore. However, a bus can still hit you, and a risk that just stays where it is still gets everybody in the end => only later. Step one is solving death => and that's EXACTLY what today's Ontology goal is about: no one has to end from any cause that engineering could potentially get rid of. So the remaining risk has to keep falling, but also fast enough so that all together the yearly risks add up to a finite total. A finite total is where the "has to" stops, and from there on, the smaller that total gets, the less likely it is that death still occurs at all, which is all that "solved" can mean for something that can still happen, and it's what I meant by making it very unlikely that death still occurs ([Oct 2025]). And then there's immortality, where death can't occur at all anymore, which is something that one can seek once death is solved, and nothing that I'd put into a goal. Stop dying and achieve amortality, then solve death and seek immortality, that's the order ([Jun 2026]).

So when I said "towards" at the beginning of today's meditation, I meant it literally. Functionally isolating the brain is step zero, the stopping of the dying, and no solution to death per se ([Jun 2026]). Most of us die because something in the body fails first and the brain goes down with it. That's why I say that this is the urgent part, and you can do it for somebody without having solved a single identity/philosophical puzzle before, as it's the same brain that simply keeps going (this is also kind of a very medical systems view btw, as any doctor is doing!). But a conscious brain that's just kept going is worth nothing if it's no life worth continuing, so input, some agency as well as protection from suffering are part of step zero itself! Mechanistic gradual brain replacement, the core of hybrid mind uploading, is step one ([Sep 2026]), and, according to my own reasoning, it's the kind of route on which the remaining risk can keep falling at all (and no, a backup doesn't count, a backup is a copy). So yes, I do think that functional brain isolation, combined with mechanistic gradual brain replacement, is probably the best shot, and the most pragmatic shot, at going towards solving death. They're both bets tho, and if a world-line truly went on via a replacement has to be shown physically (=> on the process that "does" the carrying, as a copy would tell you the same story (it's just a copy)). So all I did in today's meditation was to tell what the goal in my Ontology is, and why I think it is worth wanting.

One last thing: I deliberately stopped the definition at the universe itself, as a risk that keeps falling forever only helps if there is actually a forever to begin with (no pun intended), and if anything can go on through the heat death (or whatever other end stage it'll be) is open physics afaik => so no more engineering, "just" cosmology. So, yes, that's where I am with my thoughts after all these years. I can tell you why it's probably worth wanting, but I still can't tell you cleanly enough why I want it this badly – as well as that I also can't tell you (yet) when it would count as "goal achieved". The annoying part is that the last two get harder and harder the more I think about them – which is, I guess, why it's among the three hard goals of the Ontology!

item.title: 2/30 What Could Be Hybrid about Mind Uploading? · Meditations on Synthetic Consciousness
item.dc:creator: Daniel Burger
item.description: Day 2 of 30, the mission: hybrid mind uploading versus classical mind uploading and whole brain emulation, and what "hybrid" means for the process world-line.
item.content:encoded:
The next item in the Ontology is the mission, which, as I understand and use it, is the undertaking that leads to the vision (and "hybrid mind uploading" is its name), with the vision being a state of being in the future described as "there will be synthetic consciousness", as discussed in great detail yesterday ([Nov 2026]). One thing became quite clear yesterday: you cannot define a single item in the Ontology without first defining its relations to other items, which makes linear-style writing in a left-to-right language such as English quite hard without anticipating some of the other items in the Ontology. The one already mentioned was hybrid mind uploading.

It seems that, in order not to stay with naturally produced consciousness, due to all the things discussed yesterday (it's fragile, hence not resilient, and above all it has to end), but in order to go into a new state that is meant to continue the same process world-line, just no longer naturally produced, therefore "'something' consciousness", for which we used the term "synthetic" as in "the same kind, but created/engineered", the great focus has to be on the "well, what is the process?".

Over the past few years, I've been slowly coming out of the field of (classical) mind uploading ([Dec 2023], [Mar 2026], and, as the final push, [Nov 2026]). After I had defined it to be my life's mission to solve death (as described yesterday), I first thought that the most pragmatic way is to focus on consciousness as the most fundamental thing, and then try to preserve that with the most resilience and upshots to other things ("opportunities", as I called them yesterday), and that this would be mind uploading: scan a brain in as much detail as possible, store it somewhere and then simulate it in order to emulate consciousness on a different substrate, hence a computer. This is what I define as "classical mind uploading" nowadays, btw. So I was never technically interested in other forms of rejuvenation or gene therapies, because they don't focus on the first principles of death; they keep the process world-line within the limits of biology, and they don't address the full range of vulnerabilities I want to overcome.

Now, the problem with this classical approach as described before, as some of you might know if you've been following me on Twitter in the past few years (e.g. [Sep 2026] and [Sep 2026]), is that there are a bunch of issues, which I do not want to repeat again (I once called it "dying with extra steps": [Aug 2025]), especially because those rejections and criticisms are actually other Ontology items for the daily meditations challenge in the coming days.

The important story background here is that at some point, I wanted to distance myself completely from the "mind uploading" term, as I saw all the issues and wasn't even a fan of the terminology of "mind" and "uploading" on its own. What is a mind? What is uploading? (I'll keep both words for now btw, and the first question gets its answer in a later meditation) Uploading is so frontloaded with computer science terminology, and to be fair, a term that's borrowed from another discipline isn't a problem by itself; it only becomes one when its familiar use quietly decides what has to be true in the new discipline as well, so in the minds of the researchers and people (Wittgenstein style again). I was obviously not the first person to have issues with this; afaik @randalkoene had similar concerns, and around 1998 he named the academic approach "whole brain emulation". "Mind uploading" came down from the Hans Moravec lineage, front-loaded with even more sci-fi connotations, which might be a net negative for a scientific, serious discipline.

Now, I thought that "whole brain emulation" is a great term (Randal Koene later also used "substrate-independent minds" btw), so I was looking into terming the mission with something around it, e.g. candidates such as "invariant brain emulation" ([Jun 2025]), in order to imply other aspects of the Ontology, e.g. that the thing we want to recreate has no self-standing position, but actually integrates into the brain at hand, and also that the process world-line doesn't break, and other things (as late as April this year I still called myself "a WBE person, but not via simulations": [Apr 2026]). But I had a few issues with that. Why WHOLE? What does this mean? It already implies "just" the brain to a certain degree; therefore, some degree of brain-centredness of consciousness, which might be too much of a leap of faith already. Also, brain? Why just the brain? Even more brain-centredness (and yes, I'm aware that the slide in my own Ontology says "make the brain hybrid", but the brain is where we start, and that's no claim about where consciousness has to live). And emulation? Emulation is, I guess, an even worse ambiguous term than uploading, because emulation is mostly understood as JUST a software term (which it doesn't have to be btw: [Jun 2025]), and based on my own experience it's actually sometimes used interchangeably with simulation. So I ran into a few issues with terming this mission item in the Ontology.

After a few years, I basically realised, especially when starting to pitch this to a few people, friends, investors, that using a neologism is bad, as it's front-loaded with too much abstraction. I always admired pitches of people who could just use "XYZ but for XYZ", so using something familiar and then mapping it, e.g. onto your problem space. At some point, I remember, I realised that actually "mind uploading" is a great term, as it implies, even for most people who are not in the space at all, things such as "immortality, solving death, mind augmentation and enabling a new state of humanity" and a few more. I liked that, after all. And before somebody calls that a double standard, as "uploading" is obviously a computer science term too: I keep the word for what it promises, and I drop its old method, meaning that with hybrid mind uploading I don't mean reconstructing a separate instance somewhere and then treating that copy as my survival.

But I did not like the immediate association with mind uploading being a subdiscipline of computer science and nowadays AI, and that it's mostly, and nearly only if you look at the literature (look at previous posts here: [Sep 2026] and here: [Sep 2026]), used for "scan, store, simulate" => all engineering efforts are within "recreating a self-standing brain from brain scans, sometimes even fully destructive". So the process world-line discussion rarely came up, and never at the centre, and the aspect of knowing if a simulation will be sufficient for a full emulation, or if it's even able to have phenomenal consciousness, is a recurring issue (e.g. [Feb 2026], and something more to discuss in the meditation where I'll discuss the Synconetics programme in the coming days).

So I thought of "moving the original goals of mind uploading, which are solving death, mind augmentation and enabling a new state of humanity", as e.g. popularised in the Hans Moravec lineage (Moravec's own robot-surgeon procedure in "Mind Children" from 1988 was already a gradual one btw, but its end state was still the mind as a computer program), from it being a subdiscipline of CS and AI into a discipline(s) with fewer metaphysical claims and assumptions (so fewer metaphysical commitments, and ones that experiments can at least bear on, and not zero, as the process world-line is still one of them), and to make the remaining assumptions explicit and investigate them, instead of taking leaps of faith ([Oct 2025], and for the functionalism part of it [Apr 2026] and [Jul 2026]). So I denoted whatever mind uploading via whole brain emulation used to be as "classical mind uploading", and whatever is new as "XYZ mind uploading".

Now the question was: what term to use for XYZ? As the idea (one of many ideas, as you will see in the coming days as well) is to go through/via a hybrid state of the thing that carries the process world-line into the synthetic consciousness state as the causa finalis, we will enter a hybrid state on the way from whatever was the starting point (i.e. biologically sustained consciousness) to the end state (synthetically sustained consciousness). Hence: hybrid ([Jul 2026]). And to answer the question from the title as well: by "hybrid" I mean that biological and engineered parts are carrying one and the same process at the same time, so the thing that is hybrid is what carries the consciousness, and never the consciousness itself (so please don't picture some "half-synthetic" experience here, as synthetic means the same kind, see yesterday). It's actually that simple. And by "process world-line" I mean a physical claim about the process itself that does the carrying, and not a report of "how continuous it feels" => as a copy would feel continuous too! And if this particular consciousness really gets preserved via that transition is the aim of the whole mission, and nothing that the word "hybrid" could establish by itself (if the hybrid state is only a passage, or if somebody could also just stay hybrid, is a question for another day as well). But for today I can only say this: I call the consciousness "synthetic" once it's sustained by created and engineered parts, and whether the hybrid state already counts as that is exactly the question I'm leaving open (at least for now).

What this all implies, and all the issues that I have with classical mind uploading, and what assumptions and axioms we still have in hybrid mind uploading, is part of the Ontology when we go down in more detail, and therefore part of another day (and for those who can't wait: the post distinguishing classical from hybrid [Mar 2026], the river as the border between the two [May 2026], "The Alien Neuron" [Sep 2026], and why it's harder than classical, but better [Oct 2026]).
